title: Test salvaged lithium cells
summary: Sort salvaged lithium cells into keepers and rejects: inspect them, check resting voltage, charge gently while watching for heat, measure what they hold under a known load, and check they keep their charge for a week.

materials.item: Lithium charger with a proper cut-off, such as a single-cell charge board or a hobby charger
Load resistor of about 4 Ω, 10 W or more
Metal tray with sand for charging, and a metal box of sand for rejects
Marker and notebook for labelling cells

steps.text: Inspect every cell: dents, rust, leaks, crust at the ends, a bulging top, torn or melted wrapping, or a damaged vent at the positive end. Reject any damaged cell.
steps.warn: Swollen, punctured or leaking cells go straight to the reject box. Follow the swollen lithium guide.

steps.text: Measure the resting voltage on DC volts and write it on the cell.
Sort common lithium-ion cells by voltage. Above 3.0 V: probably fine. 2.5–3.0 V: fine to charge. 2.0–2.5 V: suspect. Below 2.0 V: reject.
steps.warn: Don't charge cells below 2.0 V. Cells left that flat can grow internal shorts and fail violently when charged.

steps.text: Charge on a metal tray of sand where you can watch. Use a charger that stops at 4.2 V (3.65 V for LiFePO4). Charge suspect cells at low current, a tenth of their capacity or less, and feel them every 15 minutes.
steps.warn: If a cell gets hot, or clearly warmer than the cells charging beside it, unplug it and reject it.

steps.text: Let charged cells rest for an hour, then measure. A good lithium-ion cell reads 4.1–4.2 V.
Capacity test: connect the 4 Ω resistor across a full cell and note the time. Measure the voltage every 15 minutes. Disconnect when it reaches 3.0 V under load.
steps.warn: The resistor gets hot. Lay it on metal or stone, and never leave a discharging cell unattended.

steps.text: Work out capacity: a 4 Ω load draws about 0.9 A on average, so capacity in mAh is roughly 900 × the hours it ran. See the notes for a worked example.

Recharge the cell, let it rest, and write down its voltage. Leave it at room temperature for 7 days and measure again. A good cell loses only a few hundredths of a volt. More than about 0.1 V is a reject.
Tape any torn wrapping, especially near the positive end.
steps.warn: The whole metal can of a round cell is negative. Torn wrapping near the positive end can short it.

steps.text: Mark keepers with their capacity and test date. Group cells of similar capacity together for packs. Put rejects in the metal box of sand with their ends taped.

notes:
## Voltages by chemistry

| Chemistry | Full | Nominal | Stop discharging at | Don't charge below |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Lithium-ion (most 18650s, phones, laptops, vapes, power tools) | 4.2 V | 3.6–3.7 V | 3.0 V | 2.0 V |
| Lithium iron phosphate (LiFePO4) | 3.6–3.65 V | 3.2 V | 2.5 V | about 2.0 V |
| Lithium primary (camera cells, coin cells, lithium AA) | — | 3 V or 1.5 V | — | Never charge |

A few lithium-ion cells are made to charge to 4.35 V. If you don't know, stop at 4.2 V.

## Working out capacity

Current through the 4 Ω load falls as the cell empties: about 1.05 A at 4.2 V and about 0.75 A at 3.0 V. Using 0.9 A as the average is close enough.

Example: a cell runs for 2 hours 30 minutes before reaching 3.0 V under load. 0.9 A × 2.5 h = 2.25 Ah, so about 2,250 mAh.

When new, most 18650 cells hold 1,500–3,500 mAh. A salvaged cell that still holds 70–80% of what its label says is a good keeper. Labels claiming 6,000 mAh or more on an 18650 are fake.

## Comparing internal resistance

Measure the cell's voltage with no load, then again a few seconds after connecting the 4 Ω resistor. Resistance ≈ (voltage drop) ÷ (current, about 1 A). Your clips and wires add to it, so this only compares cells measured the same way. A cell with much higher resistance than its batch-mates is worn and will sag under load.

## Building packs

Cells in a pack should match in capacity and resistance, and be at the same voltage (within about 0.05 V) before joining them in parallel. Packs need a BMS (battery management board) to stop overcharge, over-discharge and shorts.

## Common mistakes

- Charging old cells overnight or unattended.
- Charging with a cheap charger that has no cut-off.
- Mixing cells of very different capacity in one pack.
- Trusting printed capacity.
- Carrying loose cells in a pocket.
